passages: Donald Trump will sign a deal with Denmark to take over "permanent control" of Greenland's security after months of threatening to take it by force.
In an unexpected announcement on Friday, the US president claimed his administration would "immediately" develop a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.

The reported deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland , completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns", he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Since returning to the White House, Mr Trump has repeatedly demanded that Denmark, a Nato ally, hand over control of the semi-autonomous Arctic island to protect US national security.

His threats to take it by force if necessary triggered a major crisis within Nato. The president eventually softened his rhetoric after a deal was promised that would hand the US more control of Greenland.
Greenlanders outside the US consulate in Nuuk protest against Mr Trump's attempts to buy the island in January - Getty Images/Sean Gallup
The Danish prime minister said Denmark and Greenland expected to sign the deal next week at the United Nations General Assembly.
Mette Frederiksen insisted the deal would "strengthen security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Mr Trump mentioned.
In a statement she said "the agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people's right "to self-determination".
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, said the deal with the US "strengthens" the territory's security.
Mr Trump emphasised that "there will be NO COST to the United States".

"At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," he said.

"Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."
The deal, which Mr Trump claimed was an "Infinite Life Agreement", would stop well short of the president's long-held dream of acquiring the island for the US.
A US state department official clarified that the deal guarantees the US has "complete ability to do what it deems is necessary".

The official told Agence France-Presse: "This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors."
Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, hailed a "historic deal" and a "huge win" for the United States.

Earlier on Friday, Reuters reported that the two countries were closing in on a deal for the island that would result in an increased US military presence. However, it did not suggest the US would gain control over the entirety of Greenland's security.
Mr Trump is believed to be eyeing the mineral-rich island to provide the US with a strategic supply of the materials needed to build weapons, should it go to war with China.
Nato also launched a special mission in the Arctic aimed at countering the threats posed by Russia and China in the region.
In July, The Telegraph reported that Mr Trump had taken a harder line in talks over Greenland and was pushing to purchase the island. Copenhagen has repeatedly stated the island is not for sale.

passages: President Trump said Friday he has struck a deal to give the United States "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," following a push by the president to boost the U.S.' influence over the Arctic island — or, if possible, take it over.
The governments of Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the semi-autonomous island, confirmed they reached a deal with the United States.

The agreement is expected to be signed in New York City on Tuesday, when scores of world leaders will be in town for the United Nations General Assembly, two U.S. officials told CBS News.Details are sparse, but the deal does not appear to constitute an outright U.S. takeover of the territory — an idea Mr.

Trump had previously backed, rattling Denmark and other NATO members.A State Department official told CBS News the U.S. was guaranteed permanent access to the island and overflight rights, allowing the military to potentially increase the number of bases.

The deal also blocks non-NATO members from establishing military bases, and restricts American adversaries from making sensitive investments in Greenland, the official said.The deal is set to remain in place permanently, "even if Greenland becomes a fully independent country," the State Department official said.Mr.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that he plans to boost the U.S.' presence in Greenland.

The island has hosted a U.S. base on its western coast since the 1950s."We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many," Mr.

"We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction."Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the deal a "huge win.""Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," he said in a statement.
"This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland."Mr.

Trump has argued since his first term that the U.S. needs control over Greenland, citing its position in a strategically important corner of the world, in between North America and Europe and across the thawing Arctic Ocean from Russia.

passages: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday became the latest politician to push for stronger artificial intelligence regulations following claims from AI experts that the technology could lead to widespread death and destruction.
Newsom issued an executive order for the creation of a panel to recommend safety rules, including the development of a possible "kill switch" for AI programs that go rogue.
It was a striking turn for the governor, who two years ago vetoed a bill that would have required AI companies to develop such a switch.
Connor Leahy, U.S. executive director of the nonprofit ControlAI, said Newsom's order shows "the conversation on AI is changing so quickly."
"It's becoming extremely clear that action is desperately needed," said Leahy.
Newsom's order comes a day after Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro made a similar plea for AI safeguards , including third-party oversight and greater transparency.
TechNet, which represents leaders of major technology firms, remains committed to working with Newsom, said Robert Boykin, an executive director.
"TechNet agrees that recognizing and addressing the genuine risks associated with AI is crucial to its responsible development," Boykin said.
While some tech executives such as Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei have called for an immediate slowdown in the pace of AI development, others say concerns AI will kill humans are overblown.

President Trump has dismissed apocalyptic warnings about AI as a "hoax" and expressed fears that American companies will fall behind in a technology race with China. Newsom has said he's tried to strike a balance between fostering innovation and placing restrictions on AI as it reshapes work and people's personal lives.
With technology advancing quickly, regulators are trying to keep up while also facing pressure not to stifle innovation.

Tech companies deal with a patchwork of rules across different states and countries. Executives including Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, have said publicly that no new regulation is needed. Instead, they argue that company leaders should hold themselves accountable as an industry and not release unsafe products.

A researcher for AI company Anthropic said earlier this month that he left the firm over concerns that AI companies, including OpenAI, for whom he also worked, are "gambling with our lives" as they race ahead to improve AI that could surpass human intelligence.
The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a social media post: "People building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

State Sen. Christopher Cabaldon (D-West Sacramento), who chairs the state committee overseeing technology issues, told The Times he'll hold hearings on artificial intelligence this fall. Those meetings were planned before the recent warnings about AI's dangers, but will be informed by the events of the last few weeks, he said.
He said the state's rules around AI don't go far enough.
"We regulate your barber or your sandwich shop more than we regulate [a company] telling us that they may be ending humanity," he said.
Any new laws could have a disproportionate effect on the global tech industry because many top AI companies are based in California.
There are still questions about how a kill switch would work.
In a video about the executive order, Newsom said an AI kill switch "means a lot of things depending on who you talk to."
"We want to flesh out exactly what that means and how to come up with a framework that works," he said.

AI expert Geoffrey Hinton, who won a Nobel Prize in 2024 for his work on machine learning, expressed doubt on CNN this week that a kill switch would be effective since AI would "persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch." The risk, he said, is "AI itself getting much more intelligent and taking over."
A proposed law in 2024 by state Sen. Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) would have required tech firms to be able to turn off the AI models they directly control if things go awry.
Newsom, in his veto message at the time, cited concerns about stifling innovation and said smaller AI models, which would have been exempt from the law, could also be dangerous.
The governor on Friday said he felt compelled to act because Trump and the Republican-led Congress have not.

"There's still no comprehensive federal law, none, requiring AI companies to report dangerous incidences when they happen, and President Trump has rejected calls for new regulation. No new regulation. Let it rip. He's dead wrong," the governor said on his podcast, " This is Gavin Newsom ," which posted Friday.
Wiener, in a statement Friday, said that "California must not repeat the mistakes of Washington," referring to Congress' decision to forgo considering new laws this fall over artificial intelligence.

"We have the ability to get ahead of AI risks by setting strong guardrails," Wiener said. "The Governor's executive order is a challenge to all of us to take AI risk seriously, and the Legislature must follow with strong guardrails early next year."
ControlAI's Leahy described a kill switch as a needed stopgap, but said the more pressing issue is an international ban on superintelligence.

"Once we achieve superintelligence, there's kind of nothing we can do," said Leahy, describing scenarios of humans losing control of financial markets, military weapons and ultimately their lives because of AI systems.
Superintelligence could emerge from the process of what's known as recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems begin autonomously designing and developing their own successors, he said.
"Unfortunately, companies such as Anthropic are quite openly bragging about the fact that they are pursuing RSI and are getting very close to it," he said.
Anthropic, which announced Thursday that its Claude AI model is helping develop the next version of Claude, didn't immediately provide a response to Leahy's statement.
The protesters gathered as the sun set on Sept. 18, three days after the Kennedy Center's Trump-appointed board voted to close it for two years.

A Sikh truck driver was stabbed more than a dozen times in an unprovoked attack by a man at a Wyoming rest stop, according to local officials, raising an alarm among Asian American advocates who are warning about inflammatory rhetoric against South Asian truckers.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday ordered the formation of a panel to come up with safety regulations for the state’s artificial intelligence companies, including the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that go rogue.

Newsom issued an executive order to convene “a group of world-leading experts” to provide a “guide” for the state to bolster its laws around AI security, according to a statement from the governor’s office.
The panel could consider proposals for independent third parties to write safety plans or for companies to develop an emergency shutoff.
Newsom, who is considering a 2028 run for president, two years ago vetoed a state bill that would have mandated a kill switch.

Some Democratic and Republican leaders around the country are scrambling to come up with safety proposals after employees at AI companies recently warned that the technology could create catastrophe, including ending humanity.

A researcher for AI company Anthropic said he left the company over concerns that AI companies, including OpenAI, are “gambling with our lives” as they race ahead to improve AI that could surpass human intelligence.
The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a social media post: “People building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

State Sen. Christopher Cabaldon, a West Sacramento Democrat who chairs the state committee overseeing technology issues, told the Los Angeles Times he’ll hold hearings on artificial intelligence this fall. Those meetings were planned before the recent warnings about AI’s dangers, but will be informed by the events of the last few weeks, he said.
He said the state’s rules around AI don’t go far enough.
“We regulate your barber or your sandwich shop more than we regulate (a company) telling us that they may be ending humanity,” he said.
Any new laws could have a disproportionate effect on the global tech industry because many top AI companies are based in California.

AI expert Geoffrey Hinton, who won a Nobel Prize in 2024 for his work on machine learning, expressed doubt on CNN this week that a “kill switch” would be effective since AI would “persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch.”
The risk, he said, is “AI itself getting much more intelligent and taking over.”
A proposed law in 2024 by state Sen. Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat, would have required tech firms to be able to turn off the AI models they directly control if things go awry.

Newsom, in his veto message at the time, cited concerns about stifling innovation. He also expressed concern that smaller AI models, which would have been exempt from the law, could also be dangerous.

Wiener, in a statement Friday, said that “California must not repeat the mistakes of Washington,” referring to Congress’ decision to forgo considering new laws this fall that would regulate artificial intelligence.

“We have the ability to get ahead of AI risks by setting strong guardrails,” Wiener said. “The Governor’s executive order is a challenge to all of us to take AI risk seriously, and the Legislature must follow with strong guardrails early next year.”

Newsom has faced criticism that he sides too often with Meta, Google and other power players in the tech industry. At the same time, some of those same companies have opposed recent legislation backed by the governor.

Newsom’s initial rise in politics, as a county supervisor and then mayor of San Francisco, coincided with the tech boom of the 1990s and led to his close ties to some of the titans of the California tech industry. Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and Intel co-founder Gordon Moore attended Newsom’s Montana wedding in 2008.

Newsom for years has insisted he is trying to balance the critical role tech companies play in California’s economy and potential harms they may pose, especially with the effects of social media on children.

“I want to maintain our dominance. I want to maintain our innovation,” Newsom said at a Salesforce conference on AI in 2024. “At the same time, you feel a deep sense of responsibility to address some of those more extreme concerns that I think many of us have — even the biggest and strongest promoters of this technology have — and that’s a difficult place to land.”

Earlier this month Newsom signed more than 10 bills aimed at keeping young people safe online, including Senate Bill 1119, which would require companion chatbot operators to assess risks, notify parents in certain cases if their child threatened to harm themselves, and take other safety steps.

The governor also signed Assembly Bill 1709, which will bar certain online platforms from providing an “addictive feature” such as autoplay and feeds that display recommended content to users under 16 years old. Tech industry groups opposed the bill, raising concerns that it could cut off access to social media’s benefits, such as people’s ability to connect with family and friends.

passages: Disney is looking to increase its foothold in the technology space with its latest hire.

The media giant said Friday it hired Karandeep Anand, most recently CEO of Character.AI , effective Oct. 2 as senior executive vice president and chief technology officer. The newly created position in the Mouse House's C-suite will report directly to CEO Josh D'Amaro .
The leadership expansion comes months after D'Amaro took the top post at Disney and emphasized the need to embrace technology to advance all parts of the company.

Disney said Anand will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data and artificial intelligence platforms, product and engineering at Disney, and will work across across various tech teams to "further modernize how Disney builds and delivers technology company-wide."

"Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology and AI, and will be a vital addition to Disney's senior leadership team as we further our three priorities: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney," D'Amaro said in Friday's release.
D'Amaro's immediate goal has been to maintain Disney's momentum in its core growth areas -- particularly streaming and parks, which have helped lift the company's earnings in recent quarters .

In March D'Amaro outlined his strategy and focused on the importance of Disney's storytelling and intellectual property to all parts of the business, as well as expanding its concentration in tech to fuel growth. Since then, the CEO has made various moves to show his focus on that initiative.

The company's streaming service, Disney+, has been at the center of such plans. D'Amaro has said Disney is considering a free, ad-supported tier for its Disney+ streaming service as a so-called "front porch" to get more consumers onto the platform.
On Thursday, Disney also named Adam Smith as chairman of its direct-to-consumer for Disney Entertainment, overseeing the streaming business.

Executives have also teased that streaming and shopping will be integrated on Disney+, and more details are expected to come in the spring. At an investor conference earlier this month, CFO Hugh Johnston called it an "integrated ecosystem" under the Disney+ banner, which would bring together TV and film content with consumer products, Disney's parks and cruises, and interacting with Disney's library of intellectual property in various ways, including gaming.

Anand comes to Disney after overseeing Character.AI, a platform that allows users to create and interact with character-based chatbots. In addition to Anand, Disney is hiring members from Character.AI's technical team.

Disney said Friday that Anand managed Character.AI through a "period of explosive growth, building one of the most engaged consumer-AI audiences in the world, while also making user trust and safety a priority at the platform." Anand has also held positions at financial tech company Brex and Meta 's Facebook.

Disney has clashed with the company before. Last year, Disney sent a cease and desist letter to the startup as a warning to stop using its copyrighted characters without authorization. Character.AI told CNBC it removed the mentioned characters in Disney's letter.
The spokesperson acknowledged at the time that while some characters on its platform are completely original creations, others are "inspired by existing characters that people love."

passages: Walt Disney Co. has named Karandeep Anand to the newly created role of chief technology officer, marking the first time the entertainment giant will have a corporate-wide technology chief.

Anand previously served as chief executive officer of Character.AI, an online chatbot platform that allows users to interact with artificially created characters. Disney has had chief technology officers for individual business units, but not in a company-wide role.
Anand holds a Computer Science degree from the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad.

Disney’s new CEO, Josh D’Amaro, has made technology a priority as the company looks to expand its digital offerings. In his previous role as head of theme parks and cruises, D’Amaro led Disney’s investment in video-game maker Epic Games.
D’Amaro also plans to develop Disney+ beyond movies and TV shows by turning the streaming service into a hub for gaming and other experiences.
Before joining Character.AI, Anand worked at Microsoft Corp. and Facebook, where he served as vice president for ads and business products.

“Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology and AI, and will be a vital addition to Disney’s senior leadership team as we further our three priorities: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney,” said D’Amaro. “He is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what fans actually want. He also has real enthusiasm and respect for Disney, a clear sense of where technology and creativity meet, and shares our belief that technology creates the most value when it helps people do their best work.”

As chief technology officer, Anand will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data and AI platforms, product and engineering. He will work with technology teams across Disney’s business segments to modernise how the company builds and delivers technology.

The move comes as D’Amaro sharpens Disney’s focus on technology as a driver of growth across the company. Since becoming CEO, D’Amaro has emphasised deepening Disney’s direct relationships with fans by creating a more connected Disney experience, with Disney+ as its digital centerpiece.

“I’ve admired Disney my entire life for how it blends unforgettable storytelling with the latest technology to constantly push the boundaries of what entertainment can be,” Anand said. “I’m honored to join a team with such extraordinary creative talent, and I look forward to building on the company’s impressive technology capabilities to help Disney connect fans worldwide with its beloved stories and characters in new and innovative ways.”
Anand led Character.AI through a period of rapid growth, building one of the world’s most engaged consumer-AI audiences while prioritising user trust and safety as the platform expanded.

Before Character.AI, he was president and chief product officer of financial technology company Brex. He also held several leadership roles at Meta’s Facebook, most recently as vice president of Ads & Business Products.
Earlier in his career, Anand spent 15 years at Microsoft in senior product and engineering leadership roles and was part of the team that built the Azure platform.

passages: The U.S. Coast Guard said it boarded a tanker transiting the Gulf of Mexico in August after the vessel’s network was attacked by hackers.

A Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed the incident after the Wall Street Journal reported that at least two tankers headed for the U.S. were hit with cyberattacks. Bloomberg News identified one of the tankers as VL Prosperity, and Iranian government-backed news outlet Mehr said the ship lost communications for 30 hours.

The FBI did not respond to requests for comment and several other agencies directed Recorded Future News to the U.S. Coast Guard, which said officials boarded the ship to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the vessel’s network were compromised by foreign cyber actors.”

“On August 21, a highly specialized team — comprised of USCG Law Enforcement personnel, USCG Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector, and FBI Cyber Action Team operators — embarked the vessel to conduct a comprehensive cyber security boarding and investigation,” the spokesperson said.
“Currently, there are no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts.”

The U.S. Coast Guard did not respond to questions about the nature of the attack, who was potentially behind it or whether the August 21 boarding involved VL Prosperity. The Wall Street Journal said another ship was boarded on August 24.

Mehr reported that VL Prosperity was flying under a Liberian flag from a port in Egypt headed to a port in the United States when it was attacked on August 7 while transiting the Strait of Gibraltar. A crew member told Mehr that the attackers were allegedly able to increase the engine speed and disable the ship’s fuel and engine-oil tank.

The news outlet cited Russian analysts who claimed the incident was connected to the current military conflict between the U.S. and Iran but no hacking group has taken credit for the incident. Bloomberg reported that VL Prosperity is currently located off the coast of Texas.
The U.S. Coast Guard spokesperson said it is still working with port operators, vessel owners, and local maritime stakeholders to “ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.”
One day before the alleged attack on VL Prosperity, North Carolina Ports reported a cyberattack that forced a shift to manual operations.

A spokesperson for North Carolina Ports said at the time that its IT system was “hacked by an outside actor or group” requiring them to enact a contingency plan and contact multiple state agencies as well as the U.S. Coast Guard.

Ports in the U.S., Europe and Asia have been repeatedly targeted by ransomware gangs over the last five years as many shift to incorporate digital operations. In 2024, the Port of Seattle refused to pay a ransom to cybercriminals that caused issues at the city’s airport and seaport ahead of the Labor Day holiday .

Several ports in Europe as well as large shipping companies Royal Dirkzwager and DNV were hit with ransomware in 2023 while oil companies Oiltanking and Mabanaft declared force majeure after cyberattacks in 2022 and logistics and freight forwarding giant Expeditors International similarly announced a cyberattack that crippled some of its operating systems for months.

passages: Cybersecurity teams with the U.S. Coast Guard and the FBI boarded two U.S.-bound oil tankers last month after hackers reportedly compromised at least one of the ship’s networks and took control of its navigation, propulsion, and cargo systems.

According to a joint statement shared with TechCrunch, the agencies boarded the vessels in the Gulf of Mexico between August 21 and August 24 to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised.”

The Coast Guard released several photos of its staffers and FBI agents climbing aboard one of the vessels, which were shared with CBS News . The statement said that the captain, crew, and the on-shore staff of the vessel’s owner cooperated with the agencies.

The incident is an example of how shipping vessels, oil tankers, and the broader global logistics network can be targeted by hackers. Tankers often have complex networks sprawling the span of the vessel to aid with navigation, organizing cargo, and ensuring the regular running of services necessary with operating a massive ship.
A spokesperson for the Coast Guard did not comment beyond its emailed statement, including naming the vessels involved.

CBS News confirmed that one of the tankers is VL Prosperity, a 333-meter oil tanker that can hold over 2 million barrels of oil. According to VesselFinder, the tanker is currently located in the Gulf of Mexico.

Citing Iranian media, CBS said hackers compromised the ship on August 7 while traveling from Egypt to the United States and interfered with the ship’s speed and fuel systems. The tanker also lost communications for more than a day, per CBS.

It’s unclear who is behind the attacks, but CBS News said the U.S. is looking into whether Iran is behind the hack. Iran has been behind a multitude of hacks in recent months following the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war against Tehran, which killed Iran’s supreme leader in February. Iranian-backed hackers have since launched a destructive hack at medical device maker Stryker , hacked the mass transit system in Los Angeles , and compromised over a hundred water facilities across the United States in response to the widespread U.S. bombing of Iran. CISA has called the attacks “opportunistic” in nature .
The joint FBI-Coast Guard statement said that there were “no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts.”

passages: Coast Guard personnel and FBI agents boarded two Texas-bound energy tankers last month after cyberattacks struck the vessels while they were traveling toward the United States, according to U.S. officials.One of the vessels was the VL Prosperity, a 1,093-foot Liberian-flagged crude oil tanker headed to Galveston, Texas.

Iranian state media identified the ship shortly after the incident and claimed hackers had gained access to its propulsion, navigation and cargo systems, knocking out communications for 30 hours.The Coast Guard has not publicly pinned the attacks on Iran.
Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News in a network exclusive interview that investigators did find evidence of a malicious cyber actor.

"They started out by doing an assessment of the information technology and the other systems on board the vessel, and they did find malicious cyber activity," Grable said.The U.S. is investigating whether the two cyberattacks are connected and whether Iran or another foreign adversary was behind the attacks.What happened?The VL Prosperity is what's known as a supertanker — more than three football fields long and capable of carrying roughly 2.3 million barrels of oil.
U.S. officials say it slowed near the Strait of Gibraltar around the time of the cyberattack before continuing across the Atlantic and toward the U.S.Iran's Mehr News Agency reported on Aug.

Citing an unnamed crew member, Mehr alleged hackers breached the engine room, reducing engine cooling flow, increasing engine speed and interfering with fuel systems.Rob Lee, CEO of Dragos, an industrial cybersecurity firm specializing in operational technology, said the Iranian report's details were technically plausible, but warned that authorities have not yet revealed who was behind the incident.
"The details that they published, from what we understand of these types of vehicles and ships and similar, is spot on," Lee said.
"Everything they're saying is very realistic."The next day, Aug.
21, Coast Guard cyber personnel, law enforcement officers, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the ship for four days.

Grable said Coast Guard teams had been alerted by interagency partners and went offshore with the FBI to climb aboard — one of roughly 40 to 50 missions the Coast Guard's Cyber Protection Team has undergone in the past year.She said investigators were hunting for malware and combing through information technology systems to root out malicious activity."The real thing we're concerned about is those IT systems being connected to other systems on the ship that control propulsion, navigation and other systems that are critical to the safety of that vessel," Grable added.Typically, investigators collect data that is later analyzed, and Grable told CBS News that the Coast Guard plans to provide the vessel owner with recommendations for patching vulnerabilities.

She stressed that response teams did not find any evidence indicating the ship had become unsafe to navigate when they boarded it.How difficult is it to attack a ship?The concern surrounding large cargo vessels and maritime critical infrastructure transcends stolen files or disrupted communications.More and more, modern commercial vessels run on internet-connected systems, relying on them for navigation, propulsion, steering, ballast and additional critical machinery.

"When these vessels are highly connected, they're susceptible to cyber threats," Grable said, warning that an attack could lead to "a vessel blocking a waterway or a pollution incident or any other number of safety and security hazards to our ports and waterways."The danger that a large vessel could be compromised near an American port is something that authorities fear."Of course we're worried about a collision, an explosion, anything that blocks the channel for other vessels to safely enter and exit the port, pollution incidents — we're kind of worried about the whole gamut," Grable said.The potential economic impact is also colossal.

Grable said $5.4 trillion in commerce flows through U.S. ports annually — which could mean high economic stakes for even a relatively small disruption."Any small delay, because of a cyber breach, like, for example, if a port has to shift to manual operations, it causes a big delay with tankers and cargo vessels coming in and out of the port," she said.Perhaps most concerning, Grable said the technical barrier may not be as high as the public assumes.How sophisticated would an attacker have to be to move beyond breaking into a computer network to manipulating machinery aboard a modern tanker?"Not necessarily that sophisticated," Grable told CBS News.

passages: The Coast Guard and FBI are investigating after two oil tankers bound for the U.S. were hit with suspected cyberattacks last month, prompting American authorities to launch investigations into both incidents, sources told ABC News.

On Aug. 21, one of the tankers, described as a "foreign-flagged commercial vessel" was boarded by a "highly specialized team" of U.S. Coast Guard law enforcement officers, cyber protection members and an FBI cyber team in the Gulf of Mexico, according to a joint statement from both agencies.

"The measures were designed to ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the vessel’s network were compromised by foreign cyber actors," the statement said.
That vessel was in the Strait of Gibraltar when it was hacked, according to sources, and lost communication for over 30 hours.

The joint statement said the ship's crew members cooperated with authorities and were "critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated" and concluded: "Currently, there are no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."
Sources told ABC News that another tanker that was hit by a cyberattack was boarded by U.S. officials on Aug. 24. to conduct a similar assessment.
Authorities are investigating the possibility that Iran or another actor -- seeking to exploit the ongoing conflict between Iran and U.S. -- was involved in attacks, according to the sources.
"Currently, there are no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts," the joint statement released by the Coast Guard and FBI said.

sources.title: Thousands of Bay Area, Southern California security guards at major retailers, tech giants begin strike - ABC7 Bay Area
passages: The officers, represented by SEIU United Service Workers West, began striking at 4:30 a.m. across the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles.
The strike affects security personnel assigned to a range of businesses, from San Francisco-based Anthropic to luxury retailers.

The guards work for contractors including Allied Universal, Securitas, PalAmerican, GardaWorld, Prosegur and others. According to the union, they provide security at facilities connected to companies including Amazon, Microsoft, Salesforce, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, Cisco and Netflix, as well as retailers, hospitals and transit hubs.

The union says workers are seeking better pay, retirement benefits, health care and improved training. It says several large security contractors offered workers a $0.65 raise over the next two years.
Guards are often among the first to confront theft, violence and threats while on the job.

According to research cited by the union from UC Berkeley, more than two-thirds of Bay Area security guards are low-wage workers. The workers' median pay is about $20 per hour, less than half of what a typical Bay Area worker earns. The research also found that about 80% of guards do not make enough to cover basic living needs.
About 100 security guards rallied in downtown San Francisco on Thursday, where workers picketed and held signs.

"We hear stories about the lavishness and the wealth that security officers experience and that is a huge contrast with the sometimes poverty that that officers are facing," SEIU-USWW Vice President Sanjay Garla said. "Struggling to pay bills, make ends meet, struggling to even put food on the table for themselves and their families, and afford the rents here in the Bay area. So this is a daily insult to security officers. And it's what's pushed them to take action against the companies that employ them."
A striking security guard who works in San Francisco said workers are not adequately compensated for protecting valuable properties.
"We're guarding multibillion buildings, and we're getting, like, a small fraction of what we believe we deserve to get paid," Max Garibay said.
Garibay said workers put their lives on the line as part of their jobs but feel they are being disrespected.
MORE: SF Opera reaches tentative agreement with Orchestra musicians; season to start next week
Garla said the workers play a critical role in public safety.
"It's part of public safety. And these are folks that are securing the some of the wealthiest corporations and in the world, we got folks securing Apple, Google, meta," Garla said.
The strike comes as security concerns around some Bay Area technology companies have intensified.

In April, security confronted a man accused of attacking OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's San Francisco home. Days later, a security guard at Anthropic reportedly stopped a man carrying a threat against an executive.
Anthropic told employees in its San Francisco offices to prepare to work from home because of strike-related security concerns.

The union representing the striking workers is scheduled to participate in mediation beginning at 8 a.m. Thursday. Striking workers also planned a march through downtown San Francisco beginning at 10 a.m. Thursday.
ABC7 Eyewitness News reached out to several security companies for comment.
Allied Universal responded with the following statement:

"While we do not comment on ongoing labor negotiations, our priority remains supporting our employees and delivering for our clients. We continue to closely monitor the situation and remain focused on maintaining safe and reliable operations."

"We at Inter-Con Security are aware of the impending strike by the SEIU-USWW against several of the other large security employers in California. Inter-Con is not involved in this strike, and SEIU-USWW leadership has confirmed in writing that our operations will not be impacted. We are deeply proud of the strong, positive relationship we share with the SEIU-USWW, which is rooted in the competitive wages and comprehensive benefits we provide our officers. Inter-Con has never experienced a strike in our 53-year history, and we remain fully committed to sustaining this partnership and labor harmony moving forward."

passages: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger is taking new steps to hold data centers accountable in the commonwealth. Friday, the governor announced Virginia's new Data Center Accountability Framework, which she calls the most comprehensive and aggressive data center accountability effort in the country.

According to the governor's office, the framework is a detailed, wide-ranging plan for the commonwealth to give communities a voice when it comes to data centers and strengthen environmental standards.

The governor also signed Executive Order 22, which would create a new AI Task Force to address growing concerns and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence technology, including job loss, data protection and cybersecurity.

"Virginia's Data Center Accountability Framework is about delivering a better deal for Virginians and holding data center companies, developers, and operators accountable. The Framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy, and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve."
Empower communities with tools to negotiate stronger, community-centered agreements
End state subsidies for data centers in Virginia's site development programs
Remove future large data centers from Virginia's fast-track permitting process
Enforce the Nation's Strongest Environmental Protections
Set clear water-use standards for these facilities to lower overall water consumption and improve efficiency of water usage backed by stronger state agency enforcement against violations
Expedite the new state noise regulations for data centers
Protect ratepayers by requiring all utilities to allocate a more equitable share of electric transmission and generation costs to data centers and other large load customers
Prevent speculative projects that tie up land, resources, and energy infrastructure by requiring stronger upfront financial commitments from developers
Ensure that costs from PJM Interconnection processes to address rising energy demand driven by data centers are allocated to those data centers
Bolster our Clean Energy Economy & Grid Reliability
Protect grid reliability by requiring data centers to meet standards that prevent sudden changes in their electricity demand from destabilizing the grid
Limit the amount of electricity data centers can generate from on-site natural gas or behind-the-meter gas generation
Accelerate clean energy deployment by prioritizing grid access for facilities that invest in clean energy, further reduce backup generator emissions, and further limit on-site natural gas generation
Make it easier for data centers to bring their own clean power, including by reforming utility charges that discourage investment in clean energy
Empower Virginia workers by supporting project labor agreements where possible

passages: Abigail Spanberger ordered the state government to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the data center capital of the world.

Executive Order 22 bans executive branch officials from signing nondisclosure agreements for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and requires a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers, among other requirements.

The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like workforce displacement and data privacy issues, and determining how existing law can be applied to AI harms.
The order represents the latest signal that states are taking data center and AI policy into their own hands as Congress and President Donald Trump have been slow or resistant to sweeping changes.
Greg Abbott have both taken executive action to rein in rapid data center development.
In addition to Virginia’s new executive order, Spanberger unveiled a new “Data Center Accountability Framework” for the state, which lays out additional priorities.

These include eliminating “by-right approval,” like the kind that existed in Loudoun County for many years allowing developers to build on certain land without additional approvals, removing some state subsidies, establishing environmental guardrails, and safeguarding residents against increased energy prices that are associated with data centers.

Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), for example, is a nonprofit that has advocated for a moratorium on new development to deal with existing concerns, and PEC president Chris Miller said in a statement that “It largely addresses standards on new data centers and does not deal with what’s already built and in the pipeline, along with the ongoing impacts piling up in communities now.”

Virginia just told the data center industry that the days of building first and asking questions later are over. Governor Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 on September 18, creating a sweeping accountability framework for data center development and launching a new AI task force to evaluate how the state should handle the risks that come with being ground zero for America’s computing infrastructure.

The order takes aim at a practice that has quietly shaped development across the state: non-disclosure agreements. Executive branch officials are now prohibited from signing NDAs related to data center projects, a move designed to bring transparency to deals that have historically been negotiated behind closed doors.
What happens to one stock can ripple through your portfolio. Gloria Finance sees the connections most investors miss.

Executive Order 22 touches several pressure points that have been building in Virginia for years. Beyond the NDA ban, it requires local public approval for any data center facility exceeding 25 megawatts, mandates expedited noise regulations, and orders a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers.

The order also emphasizes clean energy standards for backup power and sets limits on natural gas generation at data center sites. Spanberger’s framework also establishes an AI Task Force, co-directed by key state officials, charged with evaluating workforce displacement, data privacy concerns, and cybersecurity threats tied to the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Northern Virginia, often called “Data Center Alley,” has been the epicenter of US data center development for more than a decade. Virginia hosts hundreds of data centers, and the concentration in Loudoun County alone is staggering.

Virginia has already been tightening the screws in 2026 through other channels. A new statewide electricity consumption tax, projected to generate up to $600 million annually from data centers, went into effect this year. Executive Order 22 is the executive branch’s addition to that evolving regulatory stack. Where the tax and utility rulings addressed the financial side, Spanberger’s order targets governance, transparency, and community input.

Northern Virginia, often called “Data Center Alley,” has been the epicenter of US data center development for more than a decade. Virginia hosts hundreds of data centers, and the concentration in Loudoun County alone is staggering.

Virginia has already been tightening the screws in 2026 through other channels. A new statewide electricity consumption tax, projected to generate up to $600 million annually from data centers, went into effect this year. Separately, a State Corporation Commission ruling reallocated transmission infrastructure costs to data centers themselves, saving residential ratepayers hundreds of millions of dollars.

Executive Order 22 is the executive branch’s addition to that evolving regulatory stack. Where the tax and utility rulings addressed the financial side, Spanberger’s order targets governance, transparency, and community input.

sources.title: Virginia Creates AI Task Force, Restricts Data Centers - The Tech Buzz
passages: Virginia just became the first state to simultaneously crack down on data center expansion while establishing comprehensive AI oversight.

Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 today, banning state officials from signing NDAs with data center developers and creating a dedicated AI task force - a direct challenge to Big Tech's infrastructure plans in America's data center capital.
Virginia just threw a regulatory curveball at Big Tech's infrastructure empire.
Abigail Spanberger's Executive Order 22 doesn't just establish the state's first AI task force - it fundamentally reshapes how data centers can operate in the region that powers much of the internet.
Virginia hosts roughly 70% of global internet traffic through its data centers, making it the unofficial backbone of cloud computing for Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.
Spanberger's order tackles this head-on by banning executive branch officials from signing non-disclosure agreements with data center developers.
The AI task force represents an equally significant shift.
While other states have focused on attracting AI companies, Virginia is taking a more cautious approach by prioritizing risk assessment first.
Data center operators now face expedited noise regulation reviews, which could significantly impact their expansion timelines.
The industry has been largely self-regulating on noise issues, but Virginia's move suggests that era is ending.
This regulatory shift comes as the AI boom drives unprecedented demand for data center capacity.
Nvidia's latest GPU clusters require massive power and cooling infrastructure, making Virginia's existing data center ecosystem even more valuable.
The AI task force will likely examine how automated systems affect state employment, from DMV operations to social services.
Virginia employs roughly 120,000 state workers, making it one of the largest public sector employers in the region.
Industry observers expect data center developers to push back against the new transparency requirements.
Without these protections, companies may need to restructure how they approach Virginia projects.
Virginia's new oversight could force operators to invest in cleaner backup power solutions.
Spanberger's dual approach - restraining data centers while embracing AI oversight - reflects a more sophisticated understanding of technology policy than most state governments have demonstrated.
Rather than choosing between economic development and community protection, Virginia is attempting to balance both through increased accountability.
Virginia's bold regulatory move signals a new era where states won't simply roll out the red carpet for Big Tech infrastructure.
By combining data center accountability with proactive AI governance, Spanberger is creating a template other states will likely follow.
The real test comes when major tech companies decide whether Virginia's new rules are worth the market access - or if they'll look elsewhere for their next data center expansion.

passages: Walt Disney Co. has named Karandeep Anand as the company's first-ever chief technology officer, the second major tech appointment in two days as Chief Executive Josh D'Amaro pushes to integrate technology across the Burbank media giant.
Anand, who will also serve as senior executive vice president, starts on Oct.
He previously served as chief executive at the tech start-up Character.AI, which developed a chatbot platform.
Last year, Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter to Character.AI, alleging copyright infringement of its well-known characters, including Elsa, Moana, Peter Parker and Darth Vader.
After receiving the letter, Character.AI removed the Disney characters as chatbot options.
On Friday, Disney said "a number" of Character.AI's technical team members are expected to join Disney with Anand.
In his new role, Anand will work across the company to modernize how it develops and implements technology, and will oversee data and AI platforms, enterprise technology and infrastructure.
“Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology and AI," D'Amaro said in a statement.

“He is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what fans actually want.” The appointment came a day after Disney named former YouTube executive Adam Smith chairman of direct-to-consumer for Disney Entertainment, putting him in charge of the company's global entertainment streaming business.
Smith will focus on strategy and development of Disney's platforms, advertising technology and emerging tech.
Disney hired Smith in 2024 after more than 20 years at YouTube and Google, where he last served as vice president of product management overseeing music, subscription, commerce and premium efforts.
At Disney, he most recently was co-president of direct-to-consumer and chief product and technology officer for Disney Entertainment and ESPN.
"We've established real momentum," Smith said in a statement.

"Our vision ahead is clear: make Disney+ the connection point for fans everywhere to engage with the full breadth and depth of the broader Disney ecosystem." In a related shift, Joe Earley, who was president of direct-to-consumer for Disney Entertainment, will become president of Disney Entertainment Television franchise and content strategy, a newly created role.
Earley, a longtime marketing executive, previously served as president of Hulu.
